title: Alfred Burns the Cakes
text:
In January 878 the Danish army under Guthrum made a surprise attack on Chippenham, where Alfred, king of Wessex, was spending the winter. Most of Wessex submitted to the Danes. Alfred escaped with a small band and hid in the marshes of Somerset, at a place called Athelney. For a few months the last independent English king was a fugitive.

A story told later, first written down in a Life of St Neot about a century after Alfred's death, describes his time in hiding. He took shelter, unrecognized, in the cottage of a swineherd. One day the swineherd's wife put some loaves on the fire to bake and asked the stranger to watch them. Alfred, absorbed in his own troubles, let them burn. The woman came back and scolded him for being glad enough to eat her bread but too lazy to mind it. The king took the rebuke meekly.

What followed is history, not legend. In the spring Alfred gathered the men of Somerset, Wiltshire and Hampshire, and in May he defeated Guthrum at the Battle of Edington. Guthrum accepted baptism with Alfred as his godfather, and Wessex survived.
lesson: A setback can humble you without defeating you. Accept the rebuke, learn from the low point, and use the time to regroup.
source: Life of St Neot (late 10th or 11th century); Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 878
caveat: The burning of the cakes is a legend recorded long after Alfred's lifetime; the flight to Athelney and the victory at Edington are historical.
